newsitem.title: FRANCE: German minister says French selloff key to Airbus.
newsitem.headline: German minister says French selloff key to Airbus.

text.p: Germany's minister for aerospace added his voice at the Paris air show on Tuesday to the call for France to privatise its national company, Aerospatiale, as the key to industry consolidation.

Partners in the Airbus Industrie consortium are looking at ways to convert the partnership into a limited company, to compete more effectively against a mega-merger between U.S. Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas.

"We can't have a restructuring of European industry if we don't have something that is close to a privatisation process," Norbert Lammert, parliamentary state secretrary at the Federal transport ministry and coordinator for German aerospace industry told reporters at the air show.
"I think this is very important," he added.

Aerospatiale, which is the French partner in Airbus, is state-owned. The previous conservative government had planned to privatise it by the end of this year, after merging it with military aircraft firm Dassault Aviation.
But with the arrival of a Socialist government earlier this month, industry executives are anxious to find out whether the merger and sell-off will still go ahead.

Executives at Airbus partners British Aerospace Plc (BAe) and Daimler-Benz Aerospace earlier this week called for the speed up of the process to convert of Airbus into a single corporate entity -- seen as a big step in consolidating Europe's fragmented aerospace and defence industry.
The fourth Airbus partner is Casa of Spain, which is also state-owned.
Lammert said the French Socialist party had been hostile to privatisations in the recent parliamentary election campaign so he did not expect a sell-off "in the next few weeks".
But he added: "I think there will be political support. We should also have political agreement to support the industrial process".

The Airbus restructuring is viewed as a test for Europe's firms and governments to marshal forces against the Boeing/MCD merger, which will create a powerhouse with annual sales of $48 billion in commercial aircraft, defence and space activities.
Airbus managing director Jean Pierson fears the merger is aimed at killing Airbus off eventually.

In Brussels, European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Tuesday that Boeing must make concessions to win European Union regulatory approval for the merger, reiterating that the EU would not give in to political pressure.
Recalling that the Commission had strong competition concerns about the $14 billion merger, Van Miert said he was determined to pursue the investigation to the end.

"We try to go as far as possible regarding cooperation (with the United States), but it is clear that we must obtain remedies that meet our concerns," Van Miert told the European Parliament economic and monetary affairs committee.
Meanwhile on a smaller scale of corporate consolidation, two European companies announced at the air show they were merging their air traffic management activities.

French electronics firm Thomson-CSF and Siemens AG said they were pooling their activities into the Airsys ATM joint venture, which will have 1997 sales of 2.2 billion francs. The new company will offer radars, control centres, navigation aids, airport systems and satellite communications.

In the first big sales announcement to be made at this year's air show, AMR Corp's U.S. domestic carrier American Eagle announced orders and options for up to 117 short-range passenger jets worth $2.4 billion.

American said it was buying 25 of the new 70-seat versions of Canadian firm Bombardier's Canadair regional jet and taking options on a further 25. In a separate deal it ordered 43 of the 50-seat EMB-145 aircraft made by Bombardier's Brazilian rival Embraer plus options on another 25.
